id: More Blues and the Abstract Truth

prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

I back the car over a soft, large object; hair appears on my chest in dreams. The paperboy comes to collect with a pit bull. Call Grandmother and she says, Well you know death is death and none other. In the mornings we’re in the dark; even at the end of June the zucchini keep on the sill. Ring Grandmother for advice and she says, O you know I used to grow so many things. Then there’s the frequent bleeding, the tender nipples, and the rot under the floormat. If I’m not seeing a cold-eyed doctor it is another gouging mechanic. Grandmother says, Thanks to the blue rugs and Eileen Briscoe’s elms the house keeps cool. Well. Then. You say Grandmother let me just ask you this: How does a body rise up again and rinse her mouth from the tap. And how does a body put in a plum tree or lie again on top of another body or string a trellis. Or go on drying the flatware. Fix rainbow trout. Grout the tile. Buy a bag of onions. Beat an egg stiff. Yes, how does the cat continue to lick itself from toenail to tailhole. And how does a body break bread with the word when the word has broken. Again. And. Again. With the wine. And the loaf. And the excellent glass of the body. And she says, Even. If. The. Sky. Is. Falling. My. Peace. Rose. Is. In. Bloom.

Keywords: The, Call, Grandmother

outputs.L1:
I back the car over something large and soft; in dreams, hair appears on my chest. The paperboy comes to collect, accompanied by a pit bull. I call Grandmother, and she says, “Well, you know, death is death and none other.” In the mornings, we are in the dark; even at the end of June, the zucchini remain on the sill. I ring Grandmother for advice, and she says, “Oh, you know, I used to grow so many things.”

Then there is the frequent bleeding, the tender nipples, and the rot beneath the floormat. If I am not facing a cold-eyed doctor, I am dealing with another gouging mechanic. Grandmother says, “Thanks to the blue rugs and Eileen Briscoe’s elms, the house keeps cool.” Well. Then.

You say, “Grandmother, let me ask you this: How does a body rise up again and rinse her mouth at the tap? And how does a body plant a plum tree, or lie again on top of another body, or string a trellis? Or go on drying the flatware? Fix rainbow trout? Grout the tile? Buy a bag of onions? Beat an egg stiff? Yes, how does the cat continue to lick itself from toenail to tailhole? And how does a body break bread with the word when the word has broken. Again. And again. With the wine. And the loaf. And the excellent glass of the body?”

And she says, “Even. If. The. Sky. Is. Falling. My. Peace. Rose. Is. In. Bloom.”
outputs.L2: I reverse the car onto something big and yielding; in my dreams, hair sprouts across my chest. The boy who delivers the paper arrives to be paid, bringing a pit bull with him. I phone Grandmother, and she tells me, “Well, you understand, death is death and nothing else.” Each morning we sit in darkness; even though June is nearly over, the zucchini still rest along the windowsill. I call Grandmother to ask what she thinks, and she says, “Oh, you know, I once grew all sorts of things.” After that come the repeated bleeding, the soreness in the nipples, and the decay beneath the car mat. When it isn’t some icy, unsympathetic doctor, it’s another mechanic taking me for all he can. Grandmother says the house stays cool because of the blue rugs and Eileen Briscoe’s elm trees. Well. So. You say, “Grandmother, let me ask you just one thing: how does a body get up once more and wash out her mouth at the faucet? How does a body plant a plum tree, or lie again over another body, or tie up a trellis? How does she keep polishing the silverware? Cook rainbow trout? Fill the gaps in the tile? Purchase a sack of onions? Whip an egg until it stands firm? Yes—how does the cat go on cleaning itself from claw to tail-end? And how can a body share bread with the word after the word has shattered? Again. And again. Alongside the wine. And the bread. And the fine glass of the body.” And she answers, “Even. If. The. Sky. Is. Coming. Down. My. Peace. Rose. Is. Blooming.”
outputs.L3:
The text presents a surreal and unsettling vision of life, where ordinary existence is marked by strange bodily transformations, domestic decay, and ominous encounters. The speaker moves through a world that feels both familiar and deeply unstable: the home is deteriorating, the body is changing in disturbing ways, and everyday events seem charged with symbolic or threatening meaning. This creates an atmosphere of unease, as if the boundaries between the physical, emotional, and spiritual worlds have begun to collapse.

Throughout the piece, the speaker repeatedly turns to Grandmother for guidance. Grandmother becomes a figure of authority, memory, and endurance, someone who might be expected to offer comfort or explanation. Yet her responses are often plain, practical, and stoic. Rather than providing grand answers, she speaks in simple observations about death, gardening, the house, and the work of continuing to live. Her wisdom is grounded in the material world: plants grow, houses decay, bodies die, and life demands maintenance even in the presence of grief.

This creates a powerful contrast between the ordinary and the profound. Household tasks and domestic details sit beside enormous questions about loss, resurrection, embodiment, and survival. The speaker’s concerns are existential: What happens after something breaks? Can a person return from grief? Can the body or spirit be remade after trauma? At the same time, these questions are placed within the rhythms of everyday life—cleaning, tending, repairing, planting. The text suggests that survival is not always dramatic; it may happen through repetitive, humble acts of care.

The speaker’s central anxiety is how life can continue after repeated rupture. The world described is one in which things do not simply break once; they break again and again. There is loss, emotional damage, spiritual fracture, and the sense that the self may not remain whole. The speaker wonders what it means to keep living after such experiences, and whether endurance is possible when the body, the home, and the heart all seem vulnerable to collapse.

Grandmother’s final response offers a quiet but powerful answer. She does not deny catastrophe, nor does she pretend that suffering can be easily repaired. Instead, her perspective suggests that resilience and beauty can persist even in damaged places. Life continues not because it is untouched by death or ruin, but because growth remains possible within them. In this way, the text ends with a form of hard-won hope: even amid decay, grief, and disaster, something living can still take root.
outputs.L4:
The house has learned to make strange noises in the night. Pipes knock behind the walls like someone asking to be let in. The refrigerator shudders and resumes its low animal hum. A spoon left in the sink turns slowly under a thread of water, as if trying to remember what it was made for. Everywhere, ordinary things seem to be loosening from their names.

I wake with my hand on my chest, counting the body’s signals. A flutter under the ribs. A pulse too quick at the throat. A heaviness in the stomach like a stone dropped into a well. I ask myself whether this is grief or illness, whether the body knows the difference. Since the loss, every ache arrives carrying a message I cannot translate. My skin feels temporary. My bones feel borrowed. Even my breath seems to come from somewhere outside me, granted moment by moment and never guaranteed.

Grandmother, I say, though she is not in the room. Grandmother, what am I supposed to do with a body that keeps insisting it will end?

In my mind she is always sitting at the kitchen table, peeling apples in one long ribbon, her hands calm despite everything they have buried. She does not answer quickly. She never did. She lets silence sit down beside us. Then she says, as she used to say, Put the kettle on. Open the curtains. Wash your face. Begin there.

So I begin there.

I boil water. I open the curtains. Morning enters reluctantly, pale and thin, laying itself across the floorboards. Dust rises in the light like ash. The laundry basket overflows in the corner; the plants on the sill lean toward the window with the blind faith of the living. There is mold blooming in the heel of bread, a bruise widening on a pear, a soft dark place in the onion where rot has started its quiet work. Decay is patient. It does not need permission. It enters fruit, wood, memory, muscle. It enters the day and sits down with me.

Still, the kettle whistles.

Still, I pour the tea.

Grief makes the rooms both too full and too empty. A chair becomes unbearable because no one is sitting in it. A cup becomes sacred because a mouth once touched it. I find myself arranging and rearranging the objects of the house as if order could hold back disappearance. I fold towels. I sweep the floor. I throw away the spoiled fruit. I take out the trash and stand for a moment under the blank sky, feeling the small violence of continuing.

Grandmother, I say again, what if continuing is a betrayal?

This time she laughs softly, not unkindly. Child, she says, the dead do not need you to stop eating. They do not need you to become a shadow. Light the stove. Salt the soup. Wear your warm socks. There is no virtue in disappearing before your time.

But ordinary life feels obscene at first. To butter toast, to answer an email, to buy dish soap, to compare prices on rice—how can these things remain when the world has cracked? And yet they do remain. The sink fills. The mail arrives. Hair grows. Fingernails need trimming. The body, terrified as it is, keeps asking for water, sleep, bread, touch. It keeps making its humble demands. It wants to live even when the mind is not sure.

Some afternoons the anxiety comes like weather. The walls tilt inward. My hands go cold. I imagine the hidden machinery of the body failing: a clot, a rupture, a cell dividing wrongly in the dark. I picture myself as a house with termites in the beams, still standing but already undermined. I press my fingers to my wrist and count. I search my reflection for signs of departure.

Grandmother, I whisper, am I dying?

Of course, she says. Everyone is. Now eat something.

Her answer is terrible and useful. It gives me nothing to argue with. I make an egg. I burn the toast. I eat standing up at the counter while the rain starts against the window. Outside, the garden is a mess of wet leaves and bent stems. The season has been hard on everything. The basil blackened early. The tomatoes split on the vine. The grass is patched with mud. At the edge of the yard, near the rusted fence, the rosebush looks almost dead.

I had forgotten it.

All winter it was only thorns and dry canes, a scraggle of refusal. I thought of cutting it back, then thought of digging it out entirely. But I did neither. Neglect, too, is a kind of decision. I left it there through frost, wind, and weeks of rain. I left it to its own stubborn knowledge.

Now, on a morning when I expect nothing, I see it: a red bloom opening on the highest stem.

It is not a grand thing. It does not fix the house or resurrect the dead. It does not quiet the heart’s panic forever. It is only a rose, rain-speckled and slightly ragged at the edges, lifting its face from a bush I had mistaken for finished. But its presence is so unreasonable that I have to sit down.

Grandmother, I say, look.

And I can almost hear her: Yes. That is how it is.

The rose does not deny decay. It grows out of it. It stands among last year’s leaves, among insects and damp soil, among the evidence of damage. Its beauty is not clean or separate from ruin. It is rooted there. It has taken the dark into itself and made color.

I begin, slowly, to understand that resilience is not a bright, heroic thing. It is not the absence of fear, nor the cure for sorrow. It is smaller than that, and more stubborn. It is washing the cup. It is answering the phone. It is opening the window to air out a room that still hurts to enter. It is making soup though appetite has gone. It is watering a plant that may not survive. It is letting the body breathe without constantly accusing it of betrayal.

Days pass. Some are almost peaceful. Some collapse by noon. I still call to my grandmother when the light changes or when my chest tightens or when I find myself standing in the grocery aisle unable to choose between two kinds of beans. She remains dead, and still she counsels me. Her wisdom is not mystical. It is made of repetition: get up, wash, cook, mend, rest, try again. She teaches me that routine is not emptiness. It is a rope. It is a path worn into the ground by all who have had to survive the impossible.

The house continues its strange music. The pipes knock. The refrigerator hums. The floor complains under my feet. Fruit ripens and spoils. Dust gathers after I wipe it away. My body startles, aches, hungers, sleeps. Nothing is safe from change. Nothing is untouched by loss.

And yet, outside, the rose blooms.

It blooms without permission, without explanation, without promising anything beyond itself. It does not say that suffering is meaningful. It does not say that everything will be restored. It simply opens, petal by petal, in the middle of the damaged garden.

So I cut away the dead stems. I clear the leaves from around its roots. I fill the watering can. The day is still uncertain, the future still breakable, the body still afraid. But my hands know what to do for the next few minutes.

Grandmother, I say, I am trying.

And in the quiet that follows, with the rose burning red against the weathered fence, trying seems like enough.
outputs.L5:
**The Call**

The phone rang just as the sun was setting, filling the quiet room with a soft golden light. I almost didn’t answer, but something made me reach for it.

“Hello?” I said.

There was a brief silence, and then I heard her voice.

It was my grandmother.

Her voice was gentle, familiar, and warm, the kind of voice that could make any worry feel smaller. She asked how I was, whether I had eaten, and if I was taking care of myself. She told me about the flowers in her garden, the neighbor’s new cat, and the old songs she still liked to hum while making tea.

It was only a simple call, but it felt like more than that. It felt like home.

When we said goodbye, I held the phone for a moment longer, smiling. Sometimes the smallest things—a voice, a memory, a call from grandmother—can remind us how deeply we are loved.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem in a confessional voice about grief, illness, domestic chores, and a grandmother’s blunt advice, ending with the line “Even. If. The. Sky. Is. Falling. My. Peace. Rose. Is. In. Bloom.”
counterfactuals.output:
I rinsed the spoons like they were small silver bones,  
each one remembering a mouth I could not save.

The doctor called my body a weather event.  
A flare, a shadow, a low-pressure system moving through the joints.  
I nodded as if I were a country with borders,  
as if pain needed a passport to enter.

At home, the laundry climbed from the basket  
with wet animal eyes.  
The sink filled itself with little moons of grease.  
Dust gathered on the television screen  
like a gray congregation waiting for a hymn.  
I swept the floor and found, beneath the table,  
one of your pills, blue and calm as a saint’s tongue.

Grief has been living in my pantry.  
It eats the sugar at night.  
It leaves the flour open.  
Sometimes I catch it standing in my robe,  
warming its hands over the stove.

Grandmother said, Don’t make a church out of suffering.  
She said, If you’re going to cry, peel the potatoes first.  
She said, The dead don’t need your whole life, baby.  
They need a candle, a joke, and for you to keep your teeth brushed.

She was blunt as a cast-iron skillet,  
holy as a mop bucket.  
She believed in bleach, beans, and telling the truth  
before it curdled in the mouth.  
When illness bent me double,  
she told me to sit down, then told me to get up.  
Both were mercy.

I confess: some mornings I wanted the house  
to become a shipwreck.  
I wanted the dishes to grow fins and escape.  
I wanted my own name to leave me  
like steam leaving soup.  
I wanted to be forgiven for being tired  
of being brave.

But the towels still needed folding.  
The trash still had its dark little sermon.  
The plants on the windowsill lifted their green hands  
with no understanding of tragedy.  
And there, in the yard, absurd and obedient,  
the peace rose opened its soft yellow throat  
as if the world had not misplaced its mind.

So I carried the broom like a scepter.  
I swallowed the medicine.  
I lit the candle.  
I laughed once, badly, but enough.  
I told grief it could stay for supper  
but not sleep in my bed.

Grandmother’s voice came through the walls:  
Girl, live anyway.

Even. If. The. Sky. Is. Falling. My. Peace. Rose. Is. In. Bloom.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a fragmented lyric essay-poem where a speaker keeps calling their grandmother for guidance while ordinary life, bodily symptoms, car trouble, and religious imagery collapse into one another.
counterfactuals.output:
**CALL LOG WITH SAINTS, GASOLINE, AND THE BODY**

I keep calling my grandmother.

Not because she answers, though sometimes the line clicks and breathes.

Not because I believe in the dead having minutes left.

Because I don’t know how to live in the ordinary weather of a Tuesday,  
the sink full of spoons, the check engine light glowing like a votive.

Because my left eyelid keeps twitching.

Because the mechanic said, *Could be the alternator,*  
and I heard, *Could be the soul.*

Because last night my chest tightened while I was cutting onions  
and I thought: heart attack, revelation, indigestion, annunciation.

Grandma, I say into the phone,  
what does it mean if the body keeps making weather?

She says, or I remember she says:  
Drink water.  
Open a window.  
Stop carrying everyone’s winter in your ribs.

*

At the red light the car shudders.

The shudder becomes a hymn.

The hymn becomes my own hands on the steering wheel,  
knuckled and dry, praying in the old language of ten-and-two.

A man crosses in front of me carrying a plastic bag of oranges.  
The oranges knock together softly, little suns in captivity.

I think of the paintings where saints hold their organs on plates.  
Here is my liver, shining.  
Here is my heart, unreasonable plum.  
Here is my stomach, full of static and coffee.

I keep calling.

Grandma, the radiator is smoking.

Grandma, I Googled my symptoms again.

Grandma, my mouth tastes like pennies and fear.

Grandma, the moon is up in the afternoon, pale as an aspirin.

On the other end: a kitchen chair scraping linoleum.  
A kettle beginning its small apocalypse.

*

When she was alive, my grandmother saved twist ties in a drawer.  
Rubber bands. Bread bags. Buttons from dead coats.

Nothing was ever finished being useful.

Even grief, she might say, can hold something closed.

Even a body with its complaints—  
its rash, its flutter, its mysterious ache behind the knee—  
is still trying to translate God into sensation.

I don’t know if she said God.

She said *the Lord* when she meant thunder  
and *mercy* when the biscuits rose.

She crossed herself before driving,  
thumb to forehead, chest, shoulder, shoulder,  
as if the body were a door that needed locking from the inside.

*

The car won’t start outside the pharmacy.

I sit with a bag of antacids, batteries,  
and a birthday card for someone I am failing to love correctly.

The ignition clicks: insect, rosary, bone.

Again.

Click.

Again.

Click.

I call my grandmother.

No service.

Above the strip mall, clouds gather like elders in dark coats.

The sign for urgent care flickers:  
**OPEN OPEN OP N O EN**

A pigeon struts under the cart return,  
iridescent and filthy,  
like a miracle that has learned to eat receipts.

I put my forehead to the steering wheel.

Grandma, I whisper,  
what if the whole world is a symptom?

What if every warning light is right?

*

In the Bible, angels are always saying  
Do not be afraid  
because they have never had to schedule a dentist appointment  
or merge onto the freeway with a failing transmission.

Do not be afraid, says the engine.

Do not be afraid, says the blood pressure cuff,  
tightening its black wing around my arm.

Do not be afraid, says the nurse,  
which is how I know there is something to fear.

My pulse appears on the screen  
as a green mountain range I am being asked to cross.

I want my grandmother’s hands.

Her hands smelled of flour, bleach, cut grass,  
the metallic dark of well water.

Hands that could pinch a candle flame dead.

Hands that baptized every fever with a cool cloth.

*

Sometimes I think prayer is just panic with a destination.

Sometimes I think the saints were people  
who misread their migraines as messages  
and followed the light anyway.

There is a spot in my vision.

There is a burning in my throat.

There is a field somewhere where my grandmother is younger than me,  
hanging sheets on a line,  
white squares snapping like surrender flags.

She does not know yet  
about the hospital bed,  
the oxygen tube,  
the way we will stand around her  
pretending not to count each breath.

She does not know I will keep dialing her number  
years after it belongs to no one.

Or everyone.

*

At home, the freezer hums its one-note psalm.

The cat vomits under the table.

My phone lights up: **UNKNOWN CALLER**.

I answer too quickly.

Only static.  
Then wind.  
Then maybe my name, worn thin from traveling.

Grandma?

The house settles on its old bones.

A truck backfires in the street  
and for a second I am convinced the sky has split,  
that the final trumpet will sound exactly like a muffler failing.

I look down at my body,  
this unreliable chapel.

Stomach acid.  
Knee bruise.  
Tender breast.  
Jaw clenched hard enough to crack a commandment.

Still, it keeps me here.

Still, it rings.

*

If she answered, she would not explain suffering.

She would ask whether I had eaten.

She would tell me to put a sweater on.

She would say cars make noises, bodies make noises,  
the Lord made the world and even He rested.

She would say,  
You don’t have to understand a thing to survive it.

She would say,  
Come here.

And I would be, impossibly,  
standing in her kitchen again,

steam on the windows,  
rain worrying the gutters,  
the radio murmuring baseball and war,

her palm on my forehead  
like a small, stern blessing,

the check engine light still burning in the driveway,

the saints lined up on the dashboard,

my heart knocking and knocking,

not an omen,

just a heart.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a contemporary prose poem in the style of an unsettling dream journal: include a paperboy with a pit bull, zucchini on a sill, rot under a floormat, tender nipples, and a grandmother who offers strange consolation.
counterfactuals.output:
At 5:12 a.m., the paperboy came down the street with a pit bull on a pink leash, both of them walking backward as if rewinding the weather. The dog’s mouth was full of newsprint. The boy kept saying, Sorry, sorry, to every house, though no one had accused him yet.

In my kitchen, three zucchini cooled on the sill, green as unspent warnings. Beyond the glass, the yard had arranged itself into evidence: one glove, one spoon, one circle of flattened grass where something heavy had dreamed.

I went to leave, but the floormat sighed under my foot. When I lifted it, there was rot beneath—soft, black, almost floral. It smelled like rain trapped in a closed room. I pressed my fingers into it and felt it pulse, not alive exactly, but willing.

All morning my body seemed borrowed. My tender nipples ached against my shirt like two small, embarrassed bells. I kept waiting for someone to ring them and announce a house fire, a birth, a mistake.

Then Grandmother appeared in the hallway wearing her blue coat over her nightgown, her purse clasped in both hands. She had been dead long enough to look practical about it.

“Don’t worry,” she told me, patting my cheek with a palm cold as a spoon. “Everything that softens is preparing to be entered by light.”

Behind her, the paperboy knocked once at the door. The pit bull began to whine in a human voice. On the sill, the zucchini split open quietly, seed by seed, as if translating the morning into something no one would have to survive.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an experimental poem about how life continues after death and trauma, using domestic details like flatware, trout, tile grout, onions, eggs, a cat grooming itself, wine and bread, and a blooming rose.
counterfactuals.output:
After the sirens,  
the spoons still nested inside one another—  
little silver ribs in the drawer.

The fork kept its four opinions.  
The knife shone with no memory  
of what it had opened.

In the sink, trout:  
rainbow dulled to pewter,  
eye a small moon that refused to set.  
Someone rinsed it gently,  
as if water could apologize.

Between the tiles, grout darkened—  
a map of weather,  
a record of knees, spills, ash, broth,  
all the places the house had swallowed  
what we could not.

Onions split their papery coats.  
Eggs waited in their carton,  
twelve sealed rooms  
where yellow suns rehearsed  
being broken.

The cat, indifferent priest,  
sat in the square of afternoon  
and groomed one paw, then the other,  
tongue combing the dust  
from the machinery of being alive.

We set out wine and bread.  
Not for celebration.  
Not exactly.  
For the mouth,  
which is an old door  
and keeps opening.

Someone said the dead are gone.  
Someone said no,  
they have become the steam above the kettle,  
the salt in the trout,  
the onion’s bright wound,  
the crack in the cup we use anyway.

Trauma entered like winter  
and left its boots by the stove.  
We tripped over them for years.

Still—  
a plate was lifted.  
A match was struck.  
The table received our elbows  
without asking for proof.

Outside, against the brick,  
the rose bloomed obscenely,  
red as a verdict,  
red as the body’s stubborn flag,  
petal after petal unfolding

not because it was healed,  
but because the root  
kept drinking

from the dark.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a darkly comic, surreal monologue addressed to a grandmother, mixing pregnancy-like symptoms, mechanics, doctors, gardening, resurrection, and the phrase “death is death and none other.”
counterfactuals.output:
Grandmother, I have to tell you something before the radishes start screaming again.

I am not pregnant, at least not in the traditional sense. The doctor said my condition is “automotive, botanical, and probably theological,” which is the sort of diagnosis you get when your health insurance has a sense of humor. My ankles are swollen like overwatered turnips, my back aches, I’ve been craving motor oil on toast, and every morning I vomit up little hex nuts into the sink. They come out polished. The mechanic says that’s a good sign.

You would have liked the mechanic, Grandmother. He had the gentle hands of a surgeon and the bedside manner of a taxidermist. He put his ear to my belly and said, “Yep. Timing belt’s gone.” Then he asked if I’d been feeling any fluttering, and I said yes, especially around dusk, when the thing inside me begins tapping Morse code against my ribs. He nodded gravely and told me to avoid potholes, shellfish, and unfinished business.

The doctor disagreed. Doctors always do. He lifted my shirt, shone a little light into my navel, and whispered, “Who’s in there?” as if examining a suspicious cupboard. Then he prescribed bed rest, folic acid, and a priest with jumper cables. He said if I felt contractions, I should time them; if I heard revving, I should call roadside assistance; and if I saw a small green shoot emerge from my mouth, I should water myself twice daily and stand in indirect sunlight.

That was Monday.

By Wednesday, Grandmother, I had become a garden.

Not metaphorically, either. Metaphors are for poets and cowards. I mean there were beans climbing my spine. My left lung had gone to moss. A family of beetles moved into my collarbone and began renovating without a permit. Every time I sneezed, marigold petals came out. Beautiful, yes, but inconvenient at funerals.

Which brings me to you.

We buried you in the wrong place.

I know, I know, you were always particular about placement. “Not too much shade,” you’d say, pointing at the yard with your cigarette like a wand. “And don’t put me near the zucchini. They’re vulgar.” But the cemetery man was distracted, and Uncle Leo was drunk, and I was busy lactating antifreeze into a handkerchief, so somehow you ended up under the ornamental pear tree, where nobody gets proper light and the roots are all gossip.

And now you’re back.

Don’t deny it. I saw your hand come up through the mulch yesterday, wearing your wedding ring and holding a seed catalog. You rapped your knuckles against the flowerbed like you were knocking on the bathroom door. “Are you decent?” you asked from underground.

No, Grandmother. None of us are decent. Not anymore.

The mechanic says resurrection is common in damp climates. The doctor says it’s a grief response. The priest says death is death and none other, which was a brave thing to say while you were sitting upright in the compost heap, spitting worms into a teacup and asking whether anyone had remembered to baste the ham.

You looked good, considering. A little root-bound, perhaps. Your hair full of peonies. Your left eye replaced by a small, determined potato. But your posture was excellent, and you still had that expression—the one you wore whenever someone put margarine in the butter dish.

“Stand up straight,” you told me.

“I can’t,” I said. “I’m in my third trimester of becoming a lawn mower.”

You sniffed. “In my day, we carried our burdens quietly.”

“In your day,” I said, “people died once and stayed put.”

You laughed so hard a robin flew out of your chest.

And oh, Grandmother, I wanted to laugh too, but then the contractions started. Not in my womb—no, that would be too sensible. They began in the garage. The whole house clenched. The pipes groaned. The refrigerator dilated to ten centimeters and delivered a clutch of frozen mice wrapped in receipts from 1987. The mechanic shouted, “Push!” The doctor shouted, “Billable!” The priest shouted, “Again, I must insist—death is death and none other!” and you, dear undead horticultural tyrant, slapped him with a rhubarb leaf.

Then something turned over inside me.

Not a baby.

Not an engine.

Not a seed.

Something older. Something with elbows and hooves and a tiny steering wheel. It honked once, politely, from beneath my sternum.

You leaned close, smelling of lilac and grave soil, and put your cold hand on my belly. “That,” you said, “is your inheritance.”

I was touched. Also nauseated. I asked if inheritance usually had headlights.

“In this family,” you said, “yes.”

So now I am waiting, Grandmother. Waiting to bloom, to stall, to give birth, to be repaired. The doctor has sharpened his scalpel. The mechanic has boiled his wrenches. The garden is chanting in Latin again. You are in the kitchen making soup from your own funeral flowers, humming the song you hummed when the potatoes were nearly done.

And I am here, swollen, leaking, sprouting, ticking.

If I survive, name it after you.

If I don’t, plant me somewhere sunny.

Not near the zucchini.
